name: The spherical Earth and its measured size in the Greek world
summary: Greek thinkers argued from physical evidence that the Earth is a sphere, and about 240 BCE Eratosthenes estimated its circumference from a shadow angle and a surveyed distance.
description: Aristotle (384-322 BCE) argued from physical evidence that the Earth is a sphere. About 240 BCE Eratosthenes, at Alexandria, estimated its circumference: the noon shadow at the summer solstice made an angle of about one fiftieth of a circle at Alexandria while the Sun stood overhead at Syene, about 5,000 stadia away, giving about 250,000 stadia. His own account is lost and the method is known from later Greek writers; the length of his stadion is disputed.

impact.note: The sphere and its size became the basis of geography and astronomy across the Greek, Indian, Islamic and European worlds (reach 2, held below the lead's 3 because that descent is not yet sourced here); it changed what people took the world to be and made latitude possible (depth 2); mathematical geography grew from it (generativity 2).

events.statement: Aristotle, who lived from 384 to 322 BCE, was possibly the first to propose a spherical Earth on physical evidence; the source dates this only by his lifetime.

evidence.supports: Possibly the first to propose a spherical Earth based on actual physical evidence was Aristotle (384-322 B.C.)

unresolved.note: Replace the lifetime bound on Aristotle's argument with a dated source for On the Heavens II.14, and cite the text itself.
Find a scholarly source for Eratosthenes' method and result (Cleomedes gives 250,000 stadia, other ancient writers 252,000) and for the length of the stadion.
Check the Baghdad (c. 830) and al-Biruni re-measurements before recording them as events or as a derived record.

research.note: The source calls Aristotle possibly the first to propose a spherical Earth from physical evidence and Eratosthenes the first person to determine its size; no earlier argued case or measurement is known from elsewhere.
